meta.description: Demonstration dataset for the 13 West Africa Sustainable Ocean Programme (WASOP) countries. It combines detailed Guinea-Bissau research (Bijagós Archipelago, Cacheu region, Cantanhez) with a researched selection of marine and coastal protected areas, mainly Ramsar sites, across the region. In each of the other 12 countries, one area has researched challenges, potential activities and organisations; the remaining areas are location and designation records only. It is not an exhaustive official inventory. Every factual statement cites a publicly accessible source that was checked on the access date shown. Potential regenerative activities are presented as interpretations or hypotheses, never as validated businesses.

location.description: Atlantic archipelago off the coast of Guinea-Bissau, described by UNESCO as the only active deltaic archipelago on the African Atlantic coast.

geometry.caveat: The outline is the Bolama administrative region (geoBoundaries ADM1, from OpenStreetMap), which contains the archipelago. It is not the boundary of the Biosphere Reserve, the Ramsar site or the World Heritage property.

overview.text: The Coastal and Marine Ecosystems of the Bijagós Archipelago – Omatí Minhô were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2025 under natural criteria (ix) and (x).
The Bolama-Bijagós Biosphere Reserve was designated under UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere Programme in 1996.
The archipelago was designated a Wetland of International Importance under the Ramsar Convention in 2014 (site 'Archipel Bolama-Bijagós').
Three marine protected areas — João Vieira and Poilão Marine National Park, Orango Islands National Park and the Urok Islands Community Marine Protected Area — were created in 2000 and 2005.
UNESCO identifies the archipelago as the second most important foraging area in Africa for migratory waterbirds of the East Atlantic Flyway, and as a sanctuary for a diversity of sharks and rays.
UNESCO attributes the property's exceptional state of conservation mainly to how the area is organised and to traditional resource management by local communities.
Sacred islands governed by customary rules act as refuges for biodiversity.
Overall management of the World Heritage property is coordinated by the Institute for Biodiversity and Protected Areas (IBAP).

BioGuinea's Blue Bijagós project aims to establish a community marine protected area on the islands of Unhocomo and Unhocomozinho, recognised as sanctuaries for juvenile sea turtles (proposal, not yet designated).

livelihoods.text: Agriculture, forest use, animal husbandry, fishing, shell gathering and ecological tourism are the main activities of island communities.
The Bijagó production system is based mainly on natural palm groves, rice and sea products.
Shellfish are the principal source of animal protein for island communities.
Tourism in the archipelago has developed over recent decades but remains limited.

ecosystems.text: The site features mangroves, mudflats and intertidal zones vital for marine life.
Intertidal mud and sand flats are among the Ramsar wetland types recorded for the archipelago.
Shallow marine waters are a recorded Ramsar wetland type of the archipelago.
Estuarine waters are a recorded Ramsar wetland type of the archipelago.
Key intertidal areas include extensive, highly productive seagrass beds.
On land, the islands have palm groves, littoral woodland savannas and semi-dry forests.

verification.note: Designations, key ecological facts and livelihoods checked against UNESCO, Ramsar, IBAP and BioGuinea sources. The map outline is an administrative proxy, not a designated-site boundary.

territories.name: Orango Islands National Park
territories.localName: Parque Nacional das Ilhas de Orango

location.description: In the extreme south-west of the Bijagós Archipelago.

geometry.caveat: Shown as a reference point from Wikidata. The official boundary is not shown: it is held in WDPA/Protected Planet, which was not used because its terms restrict redistribution.

overview.text: Created in 2000, Orango National Park is a core area of the Bolama-Bijagós Biosphere Reserve and is classified as IUCN Category II.
The archipelago, notably Orango, hosts hippopotamuses that live in seawater on an almost permanent basis — according to UNESCO, the only place in the world where the species does so.
Five of the world's seven sea turtle species frequent the park's beaches.
The park is also home to several monkey species, African manatees and several reptile species.
The park includes 33 villages with an estimated 3,369 inhabitants, mainly of the Bijagó ethnic group.

livelihoods.text: Activities in the park include farming (rice, oil palm and cashew), shellfish gathering, fishing and crafts.
A community guest house in the village of Anôr serves as a base for visitors to this part of Orango Island.

ecosystems.text: The park's beaches are used by five sea turtle species.
The park's hippos live in the sea, unlike freshwater populations elsewhere.

verification.note: Creation year, classification, key species and livelihoods verified. Location is a representative point only, and habitat detail specific to the park is limited in this dataset.

overview.text: Created in August 2000 for complete protection as an integral reserve, and classified as IUCN Category II.
Poilão Island is a globally important nesting site for sea turtles.
The park is described as the second most important green turtle (Chelonia mydas) nesting site in the South Atlantic.

ecosystems.text: Key intertidal areas include extensive and highly productive seagrass beds.
Mudflats are among the park's key intertidal habitats.
Mangroves are among the park's key intertidal habitats.
A highly dynamic coastline radically changes beach profiles across the park's islands, which host major turtle nesting.
The park includes shallow areas up to the 10-metre isobath.

verification.note: Creation date, protection status, habitats and turtle significance verified. Location is a representative point only. No source describing local livelihoods in the park was reviewed.

location.description: Administrative region in north-western Guinea-Bissau on the border with Senegal, crossed by the Cacheu River on its way to the Atlantic.

geometry.caveat: The outline is the Cacheu administrative region (geoBoundaries ADM1, from OpenStreetMap). The Cacheu River Mangroves Natural Park lies within it but its boundary is not shown.

overview.text: The Rio Cacheu is not a river in the strict sense but a ria, where the sea reaches more than 150 km inland.
The region contains the Cacheu River mangroves, considered the largest continuous block of mangroves in West Africa.

livelihoods.text: Communities in and around the Cacheu park practise a sophisticated form of rice farming on mangrove soils, a technology mastered by only a few ethnic groups (notably Felupe and Baiote).

ecosystems.text: The lower Cacheu River is a tidal ria with estuarine waters.
Mangroves of the lower Cacheu River form the core of the Ramsar-listed Cacheu River Mangroves Natural Park.

verification.note: Boundary and location are sourced. Most ecological and socio-economic information in this dataset comes from sources about the Cacheu River Mangroves Natural Park and its buffer zone, and is linked to the region for that reason. Region-wide statistics are not included.

territories.name: Cacheu River Mangroves Natural Park
territories.localName: Parque Natural dos Tarrafes do Rio Cacheu

location.description: North-western Guinea-Bissau, on the Atlantic coast near the border with Senegal, along the lower Cacheu River.

geometry.caveat: Shown as a reference point from Wikidata, close to the Ramsar-listed coordinates (12°17'40"N 16°11'38"W). The official boundary is not shown: it is held in WDPA/Protected Planet, which was not used because its terms restrict redistribution.

overview.text: Created in December 2000 by Decree-Law no. 12/2000 and managed by IBAP.
Wetland of International Importance (Ramsar site no. 2229) since 22 May 2015, with a listed area of 88,615 ha.
Its mangroves are considered the largest continuous mangrove block in West Africa; six mangrove species have been recorded.
The park's aims are to protect mangroves as the basis for fish reproduction, to conserve biodiversity and to improve living conditions of residents.
The mangroves provide food and refuge for protected or rare species such as the hippopotamus and the West African manatee, and serve as spawning and nursery habitat for fish and shellfish.
Each village in the site keeps one or more sacred forests, which act as reservoirs of biodiversity.

livelihoods.text: Besides rice fields, the mangrove provides fish, timber, honey, salt and traditional medicine.
Mangrove rice farming here is a technology mastered by only a few ethnic groups and is described as unique cultural heritage.

ecosystems.text: Intertidal mangrove forest is the park's dominant wetland type.
Estuarine waters are a recorded Ramsar wetland type of the site.
Intertidal mud, sand or salt flats are a recorded Ramsar wetland type of the site.
Seagrass beds occur in the park and its buffer zone.
Beyond the mangroves, the landscape is a mosaic of forests, palm groves and savanna, with dryland forests in the buffer zone.

verification.note: Designations, management, ecosystems and pressures verified against Ramsar, IBAP and NGO sources. Sources disagree on the exact creation day (1 or 4 December 2000) and on the mangrove share of the park, so those details are omitted. BioGuinea lists it as a national park, while IBAP, Ramsar and Wetlands International call it a natural park; the official name is kept here. Location is a representative point only.

location.description: Southern Guinea-Bissau, in the Tombali administrative region.

geometry.caveat: Shown as a reference point from Wikidata. The official boundary is not shown: it is held in WDPA/Protected Planet, which was not used because its terms restrict redistribution.

overview.text: According to the BioGuinea Foundation, the park was established in 2008 and covers 1,068 km². Other public records differ (see next fact), so the creation date and area are unconfirmed.
Wikidata records different values: inception in 1980 and in October 2007, and areas of 680 km² and 1,057.67 km².
Species listed by the BioGuinea Foundation include chimpanzees, Temminck's red colobus, baboons, roan antelope, waterbuck and buffalo.
The BioGuinea Foundation runs a community REDD+ project in the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks, which underwent a critical review phase in 2025.
Wetlands International reports that its support has improved the conservation status of 82,000 hectares of mangroves across the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks.

ecosystems.text: The BioGuinea Foundation describes the park as holding the last areas of dense sub-humid forest in the country.
Mangroves in the park are among those whose conservation Wetlands International reports supporting.

verification.note: Location and region from Wikidata. Creation year and area are as reported by BioGuinea; Wikidata lists other dates (1980, 2007) and areas (680 and 1,057.67 km²), so treat them as unconfirmed. BioGuinea's description of the park's orientation conflicts with the map and was not used. No potential activity is proposed, because no reviewed source links a documented need here to a specific activity.

statements.text: At inscription, UNESCO assessed potential factors — pollution, fishing, navigation, infrastructure, oil exploration, tourism and climate change — as remaining at very low and/or distant levels.
Researchers describe the area as under increasing pressure from deforestation, future oil and gas prospection, tourism development, population growth, local and foreign fisheries, and pollution.
In 2014, offshore oil prospecting about 100 km north-west of the archipelago and a planned bauxite port on the Rio Grande de Buba were flagged as threats, both at project stage.

challenges.title: Fishing pressure from outside the archipelago

statements.text: Overfishing by foreign fishermen is identified as the primary threat in a conservation project proposal for the archipelago.
Part of the motorised canoe fleet targets rays and sharks because of very high fin prices on Asian markets.
In Urok, Tiniguena reports new challenges from outside resource users who bring more predatory forms of exploitation.

challenges.title: Mangrove wood used for fish smoking

statements.text: The use of mangrove wood for smoking fish has repercussions on the environment.
UNESCO notes a strong likelihood that climate change will alter water circulation patterns and bring significant changes in sea level to this low-lying deltaic archipelago.
Sacred forests on the islands are described as threatened by exploitative tourism and natural resource extraction.
The expansion of cashew, encouraged by a monetarised economy, is reducing the preponderance of palm and rice.

challenges.title: Mangrove conversion and abandoned rice fields

statements.text: Large areas of mangrove were converted to rice fields, many of which are abandoned after a few years as salt water intrudes and soils acidify.
Mangrove rice farming is declining for both climatic and social reasons.
Overexploitation of natural resources in the park includes fish, waterbirds and fuelwood.
On Dapack island, communities produced salt by boiling seawater over mangrove fuelwood before solar salt production was introduced.
Some migratory fish species have become rare through overfishing, and illegal fishing is practised mainly by non-resident fishers.
Wetlands International reports that park rangers' monitoring and surveillance have reduced illegal fishing and mangrove harvesting in the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks.
The park has been heavily degraded by slash-and-burn agriculture and overexploitation of natural resources.
The recent expansion of cashew plantations is a main threat to the dryland forests of the buffer zone.

challenges.title: Climate change, rainfall shifts and sea-level rise

statements.text: In Guinea-Bissau's coastal mangrove villages, a shorter but more intense rainy season together with sea-level rise is making it harder for farmers to manage their rice fields.
Wetlands International reports that park rangers' monitoring and surveillance have reduced illegal fishing and mangrove harvesting in the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks.
The 2015 Ramsar description lists a phosphate mining industry, then at prospecting stage upstream on the Rio Cacheu, as a pressure from the surrounding region.
UNESCO identifies extensive agriculture, overfishing and mining as the reserve's main challenges.
GIZ reports that poverty and limited knowledge of sustainable land use lead local people to overuse the natural resources they depend on.
Citing Benin's national forest strategy, IUCN NL reports a 30% decrease in Mono Delta mangrove habitats since 1995, mainly from agricultural clearing, overfishing, logging and urbanisation.
For the overlapping Ramsar site 1017, Ramsar lists mangrove over-exploitation, logging-related soil erosion and coastal erosion as major threats.
IUCN's AGeReB project documents name the planned Adjarala hydroelectric dam upstream on the Mono River among pressures on the reserve.
The same document describes the coastal ecosystems of Ramsar site 1017 as heavily affected by large port and hydroelectric works.

challenges.title: Oil pollution of mangroves and creeks

statements.text: Ramsar lists oil pollution, deforestation, overfishing, invasive species and urban expansion as pressures on the site.
In 2011 UNEP found that oil pollution had left mangroves in many intertidal creeks stripped of leaves and stems, with roots coated in a bitumen-like layer.
UNEP described the wetlands around Ogoniland as highly degraded and facing disintegration.
UNEP reported that fisheries suffer from destroyed mangrove fish habitat and persistent contamination of many creeks.
HYPREP's draft management framework names oil legacy impacts, livelihood dependence, tenure complexity and climate pressures as local realities.

challenges.title: Invasive nipa palm in former mangrove areas

statements.text: UNEP found former mangrove areas reduced to bare ground being colonised by invasive species such as nipa palm.
HYPREP reports that its restoration teams are removing invasive nipa palms so native mangroves can recover.

challenges.title: Livestock grazing and contamination of the salt pans

statements.text: A 2014 Rufford-funded project describes overgrazing, trampling and livestock faeces threatening the salt-collecting women's livelihoods and disturbing wildlife.
The same project reports that livestock faeces contaminate the water and the salt collected for sale.
Ramsar notes a need for regulation to prevent over-construction of tourist structures in the site.
The 2013 Ramsar information sheet warns that further tourism and housing construction nearby may harm the salt pans by increasing visitor numbers.
In 2012 the national environment authority lacked the personnel and finances to execute the site's management plan, according to a Rufford project record.
Since 2016 Maio's protected areas have been overseen by a small management unit within the island's agriculture and environment delegation.
The Ramsar sheet reports that overfishing in recent years, linked to strong immigration for the tourism industry, has considerably reduced fish stocks.
It notes that oceanographic researchers found the Aby lagoon in a state of generalised over-exploitation.
Harvesting plants for construction wood is described as a real threat to the survival of some species.
Locally, men supply firewood (essentially mangrove wood) and women smoke the fish.
In October 2026, residents near the park raised mangrove destruction and land sales with the park authority, according to the state news agency.

challenges.title: Unregulated tourism, timber exploitation and hunting

statements.text: Ramsar lists timber exploitation, overfishing, uncontrolled tourism and hunting of birds and bats as threats.
Tourism inside the national park is not guided by clearly defined ecological principles.

challenges.title: Upstream dams and sand and gravel extraction

statements.text: The Ayamé I and II dams on the Bia river considerably affect the freshwater supply to the area.
Urbanisation and the gravel and sand extraction that accompanies it are a growing factor.

challenges.title: Mangrove over-harvesting for fuelwood and fish smoking

statements.text: Ramsar notes that the site is threatened by sea erosion, pollution and excessive mangrove wood harvesting.
The 2023–2032 management plan reports mangroves often being harvested and not replanted, including for fish-smoking fuelwood.
The management plan describes fisheries as over-exploited, with fishers forced to use ever-smaller nets.
Blocked estuaries stop marine water and marine life from entering the lagoon.
Salt production once done on a small scale by community members has been taken over by large businesses, shutting some fishers out of local fishing areas.
Industrial aquaculture infrastructure has caused the loss of large tracts of mangrove in the Anloga restoration zone.
Severe coastal erosion has destroyed houses from Keta through Vodza to Kedzi.
The Akosombo dam is believed to have contributed to a major shortage of sediment in the lower Volta region.

challenges.title: Mangrove loss from fuelwood and charcoal demand

statements.text: The 2007 Ramsar sheet reports natural mangroves along the Gbaga falling from about 1,000 ha in 1999 to 546.97 ha in 2005.
Growing demand for firewood and charcoal accelerated vegetation loss in the Maritime Region.
A 2025 CTCN plan reports that women fish traders in three villages continue to cut mangroves despite reforestation by the WACA project.
The coast faces pronounced marine erosion at Agbodrafo, Kpémé and Aného.
The World Bank reports that Benin and Togo each lose about 15 metres of coastline a year, and 20 to 30 metres in some places.
The coastal lake and lagoon system is being progressively depleted by overfishing.
Deliberate poisoning of ponds and streams to catch fish is described as a common practice.

challenges.title: Altered hydrology, invasive plants and no management plan

statements.text: The Nangbéto dam, filled in 1987, changed the downstream water regime.
Invasive water hyacinth and water lettuce have spread in flooded areas.
Ramsar notes there is no management plan for the site.

challenges.title: Fishing pressure and changing fishing practices

statements.text: UNESCO notes that fishing has considerably increased and that fishing gear, methods and target species have changed.
BACoMaB reports intensifying artisanal and coastal fishing around the park, with crews often non-Imraguen and sometimes targeting protected rays and sharks.
UNESCO links the main threats to unregulated development of maritime activities and coastal infrastructure.
It describes the risk of hydrocarbon pollution from the West African shipping route and the petroleum industry as considerable.
BACoMaB lists mining and oil exploration and exploitation in the area among pressures on the park.
BACoMaB reports that the park is exposed to sea-level rise, shoreline erosion and flooding of islands and villages.

challenges.title: Mangrove loss from rice expansion, wood cutting and salinisation

statements.text: UNESCO notes a permanent threat to the mangroves from the extension of rice cultivation and forest exploitation in the Fathala area.
In 2011 IUCN warned that low rainfall could raise salinity across the region and destroy the remaining mangroves.

challenges.title: Overfishing, fires and collection of wood and eggs

statements.text: UNESCO lists forest fires, excessive fishing, destruction of bird colonies and conflicts with industrial and agricultural development.
IUCN noted impacts from farming, fires, firewood gathering, pollution and possibly bird and turtle egg collection.

challenges.title: Breach and migration of the Sangomar spit

statements.text: IUCN reports that the Pointe de Sangomar sand spit was breached in 1994 and the resulting island is moving progressively south.

challenges.title: Limited management capacity and unmanaged tourism

statements.text: IUCN judged resources insufficient to manage a protected area of this size.
It warned that unmanaged tourism could threaten natural values, particularly on the Île aux Oiseaux.
The World Heritage Committee asked for better waste and wastewater management to limit pollution.
The 2006 Ramsar sheet notes that the wetland's proximity to Banjul and its bisection by the highway give the land high development value.
The 2012 co-management plan reports settlements claiming land in the basin and blocked waterways increasing sedimentation of the mangroves.
The Ramsar sheet lists household waste dumping among threats.
Fertilisers, persistent pesticides and domestic and commercial waste are described as destructive to water quality.

challenges.title: Mangrove cutting and harvesting of juvenile shellfish

statements.text: The high cost of firewood in the urban area has led people to use mangrove as an alternative supply.
The 2012 plan highlights mangrove destruction and harvesting of juvenile oysters and cockles as major concerns.
Coastal erosion is rapidly altering the coastal strip and threatening infrastructure and habitat.
The Ramsar sheet cites inadequate enforcement of land-use and environmental law.

challenges.title: Mangrove wood cut for fuel, salt-making, fish smoking and rice parboiling

statements.text: GRET reports particularly intensive exploitation of the Konkouré mangroves for firewood, salt production, rice parboiling and fish smoking.
The PROMAK project describes fuelwood cutting for domestic use, salt-making, fish smoking and rice parboiling as the main pressure.

challenges.title: Rice and market-garden conversion and destructive fishing

statements.text: Rice growing, market gardening and some destructive fishing techniques add to the degradation of the ecosystem.

challenges.title: Urban expansion, pollution and altered hydrology

statements.text: PROMAK documents uncontrolled development linked to urban expansion, plastic pollution and inadequate sanitation.
The Garafiri hydropower scheme has altered local hydrology.
Few concrete measures have been implemented to protect the landscape; a protected area is now proposed, to be managed by the national parks office.
Ramsar notes that the estuary is threatened by vegetation clearance and unsustainable fishing.
Sierra Leone's national auditors found land being sold and houses built along Aberdeen Creek, which is part of the estuary.
A news report describes unregulated structures at the creek destroying mangrove cover, and mangroves cut for firewood and land reclamation.
At the Targreen wetland, mangrove loss, sand mining and plastic and oil pollution were identified as the main threats to bird habitats.

challenges.title: Gaps in the legal mandate for wetlands

statements.text: The 2025 audit found that the protected-area authority's founding law does not mention wetlands, and that its operations are limited to protected areas.

challenges.title: Mangrove wood used for fish smoking, firewood and charcoal

statements.text: Fish smoking around the lake relies predominantly on mangrove wood.
The 2007 Ramsar sheet records intensive fuelwood harvesting, sometimes in mangrove stands.
A Rufford-funded assessment reports continued mangrove harvesting for charcoal and firewood.
The Ramsar sheet records fishing with very small-mesh nets that remove the smallest fish.
A 2007 survey observed severe sand-mining pressure on the lake shore near Falie.
The Ramsar sheet records dumping of rotten fish and waste in the lake; a later grant record names plastics, old nets and manure as pollutants.
The Ramsar sheet records constant dry-season burning of savanna and bush, alongside farming and hunting.

opportunities.title: Women-led solar salt production

rationale.text: Wetlands International introduced solar salt production on Dapack island (Cacheu) to replace boiling seawater with mangrove fuelwood.
The Restoration Initiative trained women on Elia Island in solar salt production, a less exhausting method that does not require cutting mangrove wood.
Elsewhere in Guinea-Bissau's coastal zone (Oio region), the DEDURAM project has offered women salt producers a solar technique since 2016.
Because the technique has already been introduced locally, a women-led solar salt enterprise is a plausible way to generate income while directly reducing fuelwood demand on mangroves.

validationNeeded: Outcomes of the earlier pilots: are producers still using solar methods?
Production volumes, seasonality and quality compared with boiled salt
Local and regional market prices and buyers
Access and tenure arrangements for salt flats
Compatibility with park zoning and IBAP management rules

statement.text: Introduced solar salt production on Dapack island as part of its 2015–2018 Cacheu mangrove project.
Its Guinea-Bissau project trained women on Elia Island in solar salt production.
Manages the Cacheu park, so compatibility with park zoning and management rules would need to be confirmed with IBAP.

opportunities.title: Fuel-efficient fish smoking and processing

rationale.text: In the village of Plindan (Cacheu), a fuelwood-efficient oven was installed to reduce fuelwood use for fish smoking, alongside a new women's association.
In the Bijagós, mangrove wood is used for smoking fish.
An earlier GEF-supported protected-areas project funded income-generating activities such as fish processing.
A fish-processing micro-enterprise built around fuel-efficient ovens could add value to artisanal catches while reducing mangrove cutting.

validationNeeded: Measured fuelwood savings and oven adoption after project support ended
Sustainability of the fish supply (avoid increasing fishing pressure)
Hygiene and quality requirements for target markets
Up-front equipment financing and ownership model

statement.text: Installed a fuel-efficient fish-smoking oven in the village of Plindan (Cacheu), alongside a new women's association.

opportunities.title: Mangrove oyster cultivation

rationale.text: Women on Elia Island, near the mouth of the Cacheu River, have been trained in growing oysters by The Restoration Initiative.
The park's dense mangroves are spawning and nursery habitat for fish and shellfish.
Oyster cultivation creates income that depends on healthy mangroves, which could give communities a direct economic interest in protecting them.

validationNeeded: Results and continuation of the Elia pilot
Water quality and food-safety requirements
Carrying capacity of the estuary
Market access, transport and storage for a perishable product

statement.text: Its Guinea-Bissau project trained women on Elia Island in oyster farming; by 2023 they had been cultivating oysters for two years.

opportunities.title: Mangrove honey and beekeeping

rationale.text: Honey is among the services the Cacheu mangroves provide.

Wetlands International reports that the savings and loans groups it has set up in Guinea-Bissau since 2015 lend for activities including beekeeping, and describes a local beekeeper's mangrove-honey initiative (location within the country not stated).

A news report places beekeeping support within Wetlands International's project around the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks, describing hives as 'mangrove guardians' because no one cuts a tree with an active hive.
A traceable mangrove-honey product could reward communities for keeping mangroves standing. Its commercial viability is unknown.

validationNeeded: Existing honey producers and current yields in the Cacheu area
Whether hives measurably reduce cutting
Quality, labelling and buyer demand
Seasonality and equipment costs

statement.text: Its savings and loans groups in Guinea-Bissau lend for beekeeping, among other activities. The Cacheu and Cantanhez location of its beekeeping support comes from a news report, not from a primary Wetlands International source.

opportunities.title: Community mangrove restoration linked to results-based finance

rationale.text: From 2015 to 2018, Wetlands International, IBAP and partners restored abandoned rice fields by breaching embankments and digging small channels to restore tidal flow.
The BioGuinea Foundation runs a community REDD+ project in the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks, which underwent a critical review phase in 2025.
Global Mangrove Watch publishes open mangrove-extent time series (CC BY 4.0) that could support baseline monitoring.
Results-based finance (e.g. carbon or biodiversity outcomes) for community-led restoration of abandoned rice fields could be explored, building on — not duplicating — the existing REDD+ project.

validationNeeded: Relationship with, and lessons from, the existing REDD+ project review
Eligibility under a recognised methodology, additionality and permanence
Land and carbon rights, benefit-sharing and free, prior and informed consent
Alignment with IBAP and national policy
Monitoring costs relative to expected revenue

statement.text: Restored abandoned rice fields in the Cacheu park (2015–2018) by reopening tidal flows, with IBAP and other partners.
Partner in the 2015–2018 Cacheu mangrove conservation and restoration initiative with Wetlands International.
Runs a community REDD+ project in the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks, which underwent a critical review phase in 2025.

opportunities.title: Community-owned, low-impact tourism

rationale.text: Ecological tourism is already one of the main activities of island communities.
A community guest house in Anôr village serves visitors to Orango.
Sacred forests are described as threatened by exploitative tourism.
Tourism that is community-owned and respects customary rules could add income while steering away from the exploitative forms identified as a threat.

validationNeeded: Community consent and customary rules on sacred sites
Visitor carrying capacity and World Heritage management requirements
Transport, access and seasonality
Revenue-sharing arrangements

statement.text: Coordinates management of the Bijagós World Heritage property, so any tourism activity would need to fit its management requirements.

opportunities.title: Products from community-managed fishing grounds

rationale.text: The Urok community MPA is managed directly by local communities and aims to secure their access to prime fishing grounds.
BioGuinea's Blue Bijagós project targets sustainable marine resource management and improved livelihoods in the archipelago's MPAs.
Traceable products from community-managed grounds (for example processed shellfish or fish) could link conservation outcomes to income, if harvest limits are respected.

validationNeeded: Stock status and sustainable harvest levels
Community rules and consent on commercialisation
Food safety, processing and transport
Market demand and price premium

statement.text: Supported the creation and participatory governance of the Urok Islands Community Marine Protected Area.
Supports the local communities that manage the Urok Islands Community Marine Protected Area.
Runs the Blue Bijagós project on sustainable marine resource management and livelihoods in the archipelago's marine protected areas.

opportunities.title: Value-added palm products from traditional groves

rationale.text: The Bijagó production system is based mainly on natural palm groves, rice and sea products.
Cashew expansion is reducing the preponderance of palm and rice.
Adding value to products from existing natural palm groves could make traditional agroforestry more competitive with cashew expansion.

validationNeeded: Which palm products are traded today and by whom
Customary rights over palm groves
Processing options, quality and markets
Effect on land-use decisions in practice

opportunities.title: Community mangrove nurseries and restoration linked to blue-carbon finance

rationale.text: IUCN NL and Eco-Benin are working to preserve mangroves in the Bouche du Roy reserve and surroundings, financed by blue carbon credits; planned work includes nurseries, village-led planting and alternative income, especially for women.
Eco-Benin reports more than 500 hectares planted and areas made sacred through traditional sacralisation practices in the Bouche du Roy (self-reported).
Community-run mangrove nurseries and paid restoration work are a plausible regenerative activity here, because an existing blue-carbon project already plans nurseries and alternative income.

validationNeeded: Status and certification of the blue-carbon project, and how revenue reaches communities
Demand for seedlings beyond the existing project
Fit with customary sacralisation rules and village governance
Agreement of the authority supervising the Bouche du Roy marine protected area

statement.text: Runs mangrove restoration, sacralisation and the blue-carbon project at Bouche du Roy.
Partners Eco-Benin on the blue-carbon-financed mangrove project in the Bouche du Roy reserve.
Supervises the Bouche du Roy marine protected area inside the reserve, so activities there would need its agreement.

opportunities.title: Community-based ecotourism and guiding

rationale.text: UNESCO reports that since the reserve was created, projects have promoted ecotourism, particularly whale and dolphin watching.
The EU-funded AGeReB action (2023–2027), run by IUCN, IUCN NL and Eco-Benin, includes support for the Nonvignon tourism training centre.
Locally owned guiding and ecotourism services could offer income that depends on a healthy delta, as an alternative to resource overuse.

validationNeeded: Visitor demand and access
Who would own and benefit from the services
Compatibility with core zones and marine protected area rules
Lessons from earlier ecotourism projects

statement.text: Co-implements the AGeReB action, which supports the Nonvignon tourism training centre.
Supervises the Bouche du Roy marine protected area, so tourism activity there would need its agreement.

opportunities.title: Community mangrove nurseries supplying restoration

rationale.text: HYPREP's 'Mangrove Vanguards' programme trains young people and women to run mangrove nurseries, and requires restoration contractors to buy their seedlings.
HYPREP reports completing a first phase of mangrove restoration covering 560 ha and starting a second phase of 438 ha across seven communities (self-reported).
Because restoration contractors already buy community-grown seedlings, nursery enterprises are a defensible regenerative activity here, if demand continues beyond the current phases.

validationNeeded: Seedling demand after the current restoration phases
Independent verification of restoration results
Risk of re-pollution of restored areas
Whether nursery sites lie within the Ramsar site boundary
Alignment with HYPREP and the Ramsar management plan

statement.text: Runs the Ogoniland mangrove restoration and the Mangrove Vanguards nursery programme.

opportunities.title: Quality traditional sea salt from the Salinas

rationale.text: The 2013 Ramsar information sheet reports that more than 70 women derived their livelihood from salt extraction, an activity it describes as sustainable.
In 2012 the women's salt cooperative produced little salt and lost its traditional market, according to the grantee report.
Livestock faeces contaminate the salt collected for sale.
Keeping livestock out of the salt pans and marketing a cleaner, traceable traditional salt could strengthen the women's income while keeping the site in use. Market demand is unknown.

validationNeeded: Whether the cooperative is still active (no source after 2014 was found)
Salt quality, volumes and buyers
Grazing control arrangements with herders
Permission from the national environment authority

statement.text: Managed the Salinas under a 2012 delegation from the national environment authority, including regulating access by people and cattle.
Holds the national mandate on biodiversity and conservation, so would need to be consulted.

opportunities.title: Community mangrove restoration with the park authority

rationale.text: In October 2020 the national parks office (OIPR) and the World Bank-financed WACA project signed an agreement to develop and restore mangrove ecosystems in the Azagny and Îles Ehotilé parks (news report).
A local management committee coordinated by OIPR promotes participatory management with the park's neighbouring communities.
Community-run nurseries and paid restoration work could build on this agreement and on the existing local committee, if restoration funding continues.

validationNeeded: Outcomes of the 2020 OIPR–WACA restoration agreement (no results data found)
Land tenure, given residents' concerns about land sales
Funding after WACA
Role of the local management committee

statement.text: Signed the 2020 agreement with WACA to restore mangroves in the Azagny and Îles Ehotilé parks.
Agreed in 2020 to fund OIPR's mangrove development and restoration in the Azagny and Îles Ehotilé parks.

opportunities.title: Fuel-efficient fish smoking for the Aby lagoon

rationale.text: Locally, men supply mangrove firewood and women smoke the fish.
In Guinea-Bissau, a fuel-efficient fish-smoking oven was installed in Plindan (Cacheu) to reduce fuelwood use.
Fuel-efficient ovens run by women processors could reduce mangrove wood demand here too. No such initiative was found for this site.

validationNeeded: Whether any improved-oven initiative already exists locally
Fuel savings and adoption in practice
Effect on fishing pressure in an over-exploited lagoon
Agreement of the park authority

statement.text: Holds delegated management of the national-park part of the site, so would need to be consulted.

opportunities.title: Mangrove restoration with community woodlots

rationale.text: A Rocha Ghana, with the Wildlife Division, reports planting 20 ha of degraded mangrove, establishing a woodlot and training community trainers in sustainable mangrove harvesting in four communities (2021–2023, self-reported).
The management plan describes a traditional cycle of planting and harvesting mangroves along the lower Volta creeks at Anyanui.
The Wildlife Division has established a tree nursery that distributes seedlings to surrounding communities.
Managed mangrove woodlots supplying fish-smoking fuelwood could relieve pressure on natural stands, building on local practice and recent project work.

validationNeeded: Survival of planted areas (no independent monitoring found)
Customary land ownership (the Anlo Traditional Council)
Fuelwood demand and sustainable yield
Fit with the 2023–2032 management plan

statement.text: Ran the 2021–2023 PAPBio mangrove restoration and livelihoods project in four Keta Lagoon communities.
Partnered A Rocha Ghana on the PAPBio project and runs a tree nursery for surrounding communities.

opportunities.title: Community-guided bird and turtle tourism

rationale.text: The Wildlife Division is trying to promote bird watching and night turtle walks.
Community guiding services could share in this tourism and give residents an income linked to protecting nesting beaches and bird areas.

validationNeeded: Visitor numbers and access
Benefit-sharing with communities
Disturbance limits for nesting turtles and birds

statement.text: Is promoting bird watching and night turtle walks at the site.

opportunities.title: Women-led mangrove replanting with solar fish preservation

rationale.text: A 2025 CTCN technical-assistance plan, requested by a women fish traders' group at Togokomé, proposes replanting mangroves and solar fish smoking and cold storage (planned, not yet implemented).
The World Bank reports that 257 hectares of mangroves have been planted in Togo under the WACA programme.
Because women fish traders still cut mangroves for fuel, combining replanting with solar fish preservation addresses a documented cause of loss.

validationNeeded: Whether the CTCN project is funded and implemented
Cost and reliability of solar smoking and cold storage
Survival of earlier WACA plantings
Consultation with the environment ministry

statement.text: Prepared the 2025 technical-assistance plan for women-led mangrove replanting and solar fish preservation in Togo's Maritime Region.
Financed mangrove planting in Togo.
Its staff act against unsustainable logging and fishing at the site, which has no management plan, so it would need to be consulted.

opportunities.title: Value-added traditional fish products by Imraguen women

rationale.text: Since 2000 IUCN, the park, IFAD and FIBA have supported Imraguen women with processing facilities, hygiene and management training and new packaging for traditional products.
Inside the park only the Imraguen may fish, on foot or from sailing boats; motorised boats are banned.
Traceable traditional products tied to sail-only fishing could raise income per catch rather than catch volume, in line with the park's fishing rules.

validationNeeded: Current status of the processing units
Market demand and certification for traditional products
Effect on fishing pressure
Agreement of the park authority

statement.text: Has worked since 2000 with IUCN, IFAD and FIBA to support Imraguen women's fish processing.

opportunities.title: Women's mangrove replanting and sustainable shellfish processing

rationale.text: UNESCO reports that grass-roots village associations run mangrove nurseries and reforestation plots.
A women's group in the delta has led mangrove reforestation since 2007 and set harvesting periods and biological rest periods (news report).
FAO reports training women seafood processors at Niodior in food safety, hygiene and entrepreneurship.
Women-led shellfish processing tied to harvest rules and mangrove replanting builds on documented local practice.

validationNeeded: Which women's groups are active and where (Niodior's position relative to the park is unverified)
Stock status and harvest rules
Market access and food-safety requirements
Agreement of the park authority

statement.text: Named as the park's managing body in the 1993 Ramsar sheet, so would need to be consulted; its current role should be confirmed.

opportunities.title: Products and services from community-managed fishing areas

rationale.text: The Bamboung bolon became a community marine protected area in 2003, proposed and led by the Senegalese NGO Océanium with funding from the French Global Environment Facility.
IRD monitored its fish populations between 2003 and 2012.
Products or services linked to community-managed fishing areas could reward their protection. Viability and current status are unknown.

validationNeeded: Current status of the Bamboung community MPA
Monitoring results after 2012
Community rules on commercial use
Market demand

statement.text: Proposed and led the Bamboung community marine protected area project.

opportunities.title: Women-led oyster and cockle products under co-management

rationale.text: The Gambia designated the TRY Association with exclusive use rights to the cockle and oyster fishery in the Tanbi special management area.
TRY members agreed to extend the closed season to nine months to let oysters grow bigger.
A 2010 grant set up microcredit for members, who learned to pickle oysters for sale during the closed season.
TRY received a GEF grant through the National Environment Agency for mangrove reforestation and aquaculture.
Value-added oyster products sold under existing co-management rights could raise income without increasing harvest.

validationNeeded: Whether the 2012 co-management plan is still in force
Product safety and water quality near Banjul
Market demand for processed oysters
Consultation with the parks and fisheries departments

statement.text: Holds exclusive cockle and oyster use rights in Tanbi and manages the fishery under the co-management plan.
Implemented the USAID Ba Nafaa project that supported the co-management plan and the 2010 microcredit grant.
Manages the national park and assists with enforcement under the co-management plan, so would need to be consulted.

opportunities.title: Women-led solar salt production

rationale.text: Guinée Écologie reports supporting ten women's groups with solar tarpaulins and technical help in the Konkouré delta and the Mélakoré estuary in 2025.
BirdLife reports a CEPF-funded pilot in Dubréka prefecture producing salt with sunlight and tarpaulins instead of fuelwood.
Since salt boiling is a documented driver of mangrove cutting here, women-led solar salt production is a defensible regenerative activity.

validationNeeded: Results at the Konkouré sites specifically (2025 figures combine two areas)
Salt quality, prices and buyers compared with boiled salt
Access to salt flats
Fit with the planned protected area

statement.text: Supported women's groups with solar-salt tarpaulins in the Konkouré delta in 2025.
Named as the future manager of the proposed Konkouré protected area, so would need to be consulted.

opportunities.title: Improved fish-smoking ovens

rationale.text: Guinée Écologie reports supporting 98 women in the Konkouré delta in 2025 to rebuild and use improved fish-smoking ovens.
Wider use of improved ovens could cut the fuelwood demand that drives mangrove cutting here.

validationNeeded: Measured fuelwood savings and continued use
Cost and maintenance of the ovens
Fish supply and market requirements

statement.text: Supported women in the Konkouré delta in 2025 to rebuild and use improved fish-smoking ovens.

opportunities.title: Oyster farming and mangrove honey value chains

rationale.text: Guinée Écologie installed oyster garlands at pilot sites, two of them in the Konkouré delta, in 2025.
PROMAK describes honey as a little-developed value chain in the Konkouré landscape, with a few pilot initiatives, and commissioned a 2026 market and value-chain study.
Oyster and honey products depend on healthy mangroves, so value chains built around them could reward protection, subject to the planned market study.

validationNeeded: Findings of the 2026 PROMAK market and value-chain study
Oyster food safety and water quality
Honey yields and buyers

statement.text: Runs oyster-farming pilots in the Konkouré delta and the few honey pilots in the landscape.
Leads the PROMAK consortium, which commissioned a 2026 market and value-chain study for the Konkouré landscape.

opportunities.title: Community mangrove nurseries and planting

rationale.text: Freetown City Council reports planting 275,000 mangroves in three coastal communities, tracked digitally by community youth; whether these sites lie in the Ramsar site is not established.
A blue-carbon developer announced in May 2024 a conservation and restoration project covering 10,000 hectares of the estuary; its current status is unknown.
Community nurseries and paid planting could supply restoration in the estuary, if a restoration or carbon project proceeds.

validationNeeded: Whether planting sites are inside the Ramsar site
Status of the announced blue-carbon project
Land tenure and encroachment risk
Consultation with the protected-area authority

statement.text: Runs mangrove planting in Freetown coastal communities under its #FreetownTheTreeTown campaign.
Carries out enforcement at the estuary, although its mandate over wetlands is limited, so would need to be consulted.

opportunities.title: Community bird guiding at the Targreen wetland

rationale.text: In December 2024 the Sierra Leone Nature Guide Association trained stakeholders, youths and pupils around the Targreen wetland, part of the estuary, in bird conservation.
Trained local guides could offer birdwatching services that give residents an income linked to protecting bird habitat.

validationNeeded: Visitor demand and access to Lungi
Who would employ or certify guides
Effect of sand mining and pollution on the site

statement.text: Ran bird-conservation training around the Targreen wetland in December 2024.

opportunities.title: Improved stoves and fish processing

rationale.text: Wetlands International Africa supported the production and use of improved stoves with women in Fallie and Senbehun, and a cassava processing unit in Teh, under an EU-funded mangrove project (2025).
The 2007 Ramsar sheet records earlier trials of fish-smoking structures and a solar fish drier.
Locally made improved stoves and smokers could reduce demand for mangrove wood, the main fuel for fish smoking here.

validationNeeded: Results of the current project (none published)
Fuel savings and adoption
Who would make and sell the stoves
Consultation with the reserve authority

statement.text: Supported improved stoves and a cassava processing unit in Lake Piso communities under an EU-funded mangrove project.
Responsible for conservation forestry and lists the Lake Piso reserve among protected areas, so would need to be consulted.

opportunities.title: Selective fishing and small-scale fish farming

rationale.text: A 2016–2017 small grant trained fishers in selective fishing, supplied approved net sizes and started cage fish farming on the lake (marked completed; no outcome data).
Legal-mesh fishing combined with small-scale fish farming could reduce pressure on juvenile fish while sustaining income.

validationNeeded: Outcomes of the earlier grant
Environmental effects of cage farming in the lake
Enforcement of net-size rules
Consultation with the environmental agency

statement.text: Ran the 2016–2017 GEF small-grant project on selective fishing and cage fish farming at Lake Piso.
Named in the Ramsar sheet as the agency responsible for the wetland, so would need to be consulted.

organisations.name: Institute for Biodiversity and Protected Areas

role.text: Created in 2004 to protect and manage Guinea-Bissau's biodiversity through the National System of Protected Areas, which covers about 26% of the national territory. It coordinates management of the Bijagós World Heritage property and manages the Cacheu park. Its 2006 annual report records the appointment of wardens for the Orango, João Vieira–Poilão and Cacheu parks; current park-level arrangements were not re-verified.

Conservation trust fund established in 2011 as a long-term financing mechanism for Guinea-Bissau's protected areas, with funding channelled through IBAP. It supports Orango National Park, runs the Blue Bijagós project and runs a community REDD+ project in the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks. It is listed as a member of the Consortium of African Funds for the Environment (CAFÉ).
Guinean NGO that supported the creation and participatory governance of the Urok Islands Community Marine Protected Area.

With IBAP and partners, ran a 2015–2018 initiative to conserve and restore the Cacheu mangroves, including ecological restoration of abandoned rice fields, solar salt and a fuel-efficient fish-smoking oven. It reports that its support has improved the conservation status of 82,000 hectares of mangroves across the Cacheu and Cantanhez parks. In Liberia's Lake Piso reserve it has supported improved stoves and a cassava processing unit under an EU-funded mangrove project.

organisations.name: International Union for Conservation of Nature

role.text: Provided technical assistance to the coastal planning that led to the 1996 Bolama-Bijagós Biosphere Reserve.

Restoration programme uniting 10 countries and three Global Environment Facility agencies (IUCN, FAO and UNEP). Its Guinea-Bissau project works with women on Elia Island, near the mouth of the Cacheu River. The reviewed source does not say which agency leads the Guinea-Bissau project.

organisations.name: Regional Partnership for Coastal and Marine Conservation in West Africa

role.text: Regional coalition for the conservation and sustainable management of West Africa's coastal and marine areas. It partners with Rainforest Trust on a proposed project supporting new marine protected area designations in the Bijagós.
Raising funds, with PRCM, to support government designation of four new marine protected areas in the Bijagós, including three island community MPAs (proposed project).
National NGO supporting a network of environmental schools (EVA) around the park.

organisations.name: CE3C – Centre for Ecology, Evolution and Environmental Changes (University of Lisbon)

role.text: Runs a research project on the ecological integrity of the Bijagós as a key site for waders on the East Atlantic Flyway, with partners including Tiniguena.

organisations.name: Centre National de Gestion des Réserves de Faune

role.text: Benin's national wildlife-reserve agency; supervising administration of the Bouche du Roy marine protected area inside the reserve.
Implemented the 2013–2019 project, funded by the German International Climate Initiative, that prepared the transboundary biosphere reserve.

organisations.name: IUCN National Committee of the Netherlands

role.text: Worked with local partners, GIZ and both governments to create the reserve, and partners Eco-Benin on blue-carbon mangrove work.
Beninese NGO running mangrove restoration and sacralisation and a blue-carbon project in the Bouche du Roy area of the reserve.
Federal agency under the Ministry of Environment carrying out the Ogoniland clean-up, mangrove restoration and livelihood programmes, and preparing the Ramsar site management plan.
Carried out the 2011 independent environmental assessment of Ogoniland whose recommendations frame the clean-up.
Maio NGO that managed the Salinas under a 2012 delegation, monitors its birds and turtles, and leads co-management of Maio's protected areas.
National environment directorate with the mandate and authority on biodiversity and conservation in Cabo Verde.

organisations.name: Office Ivoirien des Parcs et Réserves

role.text: Holds delegated management of the national-park part of the Ramsar site.

organisations.name: West Africa Coastal Areas Management Program (WACA)

role.text: World Bank-financed coastal resilience programme; funded mangrove restoration with OIPR in Côte d'Ivoire and mangrove planting in Togo.

organisations.name: Wildlife Division, Forestry Commission of Ghana

role.text: Management authority of the Keta Lagoon Complex Ramsar Site, mandated to enforce the law.
Ran the 2021–2023 PAPBio mangrove restoration and livelihoods project in four Keta Lagoon communities, with the Wildlife Division.
Its staff act against unsustainable logging, fishing and illegal hunting at the site; it is the implementing agency of WACA in Togo.
UNFCCC technology body that prepared a 2025 technical-assistance plan for women-led mangrove restoration and solar fish preservation in Togo's Maritime Region.
Public administrative body that manages the park under its own law (2000-024).

role.text: Conservation trust fund created in 2009 that provides long-term funding for the park, including sea surveillance and shared governance.
Named as the park's managing body in the 1993 Ramsar sheet; UNESCO names it as a partner in integrated management planning.
Senegalese marine conservation association that proposed and led the Bamboung community marine protected area project.
Community-based non-profit founded in 2007 that holds exclusive cockle and oyster use rights in Tanbi; it received the Equator Prize in 2012.

organisations.name: Department of Parks and Wildlife Management (The Gambia)

role.text: Has managed the Tanbi Wetlands Complex since 2005 and assists with enforcement under the shellfish co-management plan.

organisations.name: Coastal Resources Center, University of Rhode Island

role.text: Implemented the USAID Ba Nafaa project, with WWF, that supported the Tanbi shellfish co-management plan.
Guinean NGO running mangrove restoration, solar salt, improved ovens and oyster pilots in the Konkouré delta, and a partner in the PROMAK protected-area project.
Leads the EU-funded PROMAK consortium (2025–2028) working towards legal protection of the Konkouré mangroves.

organisations.name: Office Guinéen des Parcs Nationaux et Réserves de Faune

role.text: Named as the future manager of the protected area proposed for the Konkouré mangroves.
Statutory protected-area authority; carries out enforcement against encroachment at the estuary, though its mandate over wetlands is limited.
Runs mangrove planting in Freetown coastal communities under its #FreetownTheTreeTown campaign.
Ran bird-conservation and nature-guiding training around the Targreen wetland in 2024.
National authority for conservation forestry; lists the Lake Piso Multiple Sustainable Use Reserve among Liberia's protected areas.
Named in the 2007 Ramsar sheet as the agency responsible for the Lake Piso wetland.
Grantee of a 2016–2017 GEF small-grant project on sustainable fishing at Lake Piso.
